sections.text: ## Defining Revolution

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Not all upheaval is revolution. The scholarly definition requires two things:

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text:
1. **Forcible transfer of state power** from one group to another
2. **Structural transformation** — not just who holds power but how power is organized

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Crane Brinton's classic typology (*Anatomy of Revolution*, 1938) studied four "great" revolutions (English, American, French, Russian) and found a common fever curve: moderate phase → radical phase → thermidor (conservative reaction). This is descriptive pattern-finding, not causal theory.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: The move to causal theory comes in the 1970s-80s.

sections.text: ## Skocpol: Structural Analysis

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Theda Skocpol, *States and Social Revolutions* (1979), is the central text. It established comparative-historical analysis as a method and structural theory as the dominant explanatory framework.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

INTERNATIONAL PRESSURE
         (military competition,

                │

    Old elites block state reform and paralyze the center.

    Strong village communities. Peasant revolt becomes possible

                │                │

              REVOLUTIONARY SITUATION
              (dual power: old regime

sections.text: ### Key Insight: Revolutionary Actors Don't Cause Revolutions

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: The counterintuitive Skocpol thesis: **revolutionary movements don't create revolutionary situations — they exploit them.** The Russian Bolsheviks were a tiny party in February 1917. The state had already collapsed from WWI. They won because they were the best-organized group in a power vacuum.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: This is structuralism at its strongest: the revolutionaries' ideology, leadership quality, and organizational skill matter far less than structural preconditions.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: ### Critiques

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text:
- Underweights ideology and leadership (why did Stalin rather than Trotsky consolidate power?)
- Selection bias toward successful revolutions — the model doesn't predict which crises will become revolutions
- Ignores agency of key individuals (Lenin, Robespierre)
- Iranian Revolution (1979) doesn't fit cleanly — no peasant revolt, no landlord class conflict in Skocpol's sense

sections.text: ## Goldstone: Demographic-Structural Model

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Jack Goldstone (*Revolution and Rebellion in the Early Modern World*, 1991; revised in *Revolutions*, 2014) extends and refines Skocpol with a focus on population dynamics.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Goldstone's model explains why revolutions come in waves: the 17th-century general crisis (English, Fronde, Ming collapse, Ottoman crisis) happened simultaneously across Eurasia because similar demographic pressures operated across different political systems.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: ### 5th Generation States

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Goldstone's more recent work identifies "5th generation states" — authoritarian regimes with a single ruling family or party plus a rentier economy. They are vulnerable to a different dynamic: patron-client networks, elite defection when oil rents fall.

sections.text: ## Tilly: Contentious Politics and Repertoires

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Charles Tilly approached revolution from a different angle: not why do states collapse but how do people make political claims, and when do those claims escalate to revolution?

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: ### WUNC Framework

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text:
Claims gain traction when they display:
- **W**orthiness (respectable actors, symbols of legitimacy)
- **U**nity (clear collective identity, discipline)
- **N**umbers (demonstrating scale of support)
- **C**ommitment (willingness to bear costs, sacrifice)

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: ### Revolutionary Situations vs. Revolutionary Outcomes

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Tilly's crucial distinction:

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: **Revolutionary situation**: Multiple claimants to sovereignty — both old regime and challenger claim to speak for the state. These are common. They don't always produce revolutionary outcomes.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: **Revolutionary outcome**: Actual transfer of state power to new coalition, with structural change.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: What determines whether a revolutionary situation becomes an outcome? Coalition formation, defection by state forces (especially army), and the capacity of challengers to consolidate a new state apparatus.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt
Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Hannah Arendt (*On Revolution*, 1963) comes from an entirely different tradition. Not causal explanation but phenomenological analysis — what does revolution *mean*?

sections.text: ### The Council Form

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Arendt observed that every major modern revolution spontaneously produced councils — soviets in Russia, Räte in Germany, town meetings in America. These were not Bolshevik inventions but organic political forms.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Her thesis: councils are the genuine expression of *public freedom* — political action as an end in itself. The tragedy of revolutions is that parties and bureaucracies destroy the councils (the Bolsheviks dissolved the soviets once they seized power).

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: ### Critique

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Arendt's reading of the American Revolution is idealized — it ignores slavery, property qualifications, and the "social question" (poverty) in America. Her French/Russian comparison is more defensible. Her category of "social revolution" as necessarily leading to Terror is contested.

sections.text: ## Color Revolutions and Their Fate

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: "Color revolutions" (Serbia 2000, Georgia 2003, Ukraine 2004, Kyrgyzstan 2005) were mostly non-violent transitions using mass mobilization to challenge fraudulent elections.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt
Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text:
Fraudulent election → mass popular protest
         │
         ▼
  Security forces refuse to fire (crucial)
         │
         ▼
  Elite defection from old regime
         │
         ▼
  New leadership elected

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text:
WHY IT WORKS:
  • WUNC requirements met (peaceful, mass, legitimate)
  • International support (EU/US signal recognition)
  • Security forces don't want to be on the losing side

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text:
WHY IT FAILS:
  • Security forces loyal (Belarus 2020, Burma 2021)
  • Old elites reconsolidate (Kyrgyzstan after 2005)
  • No institutional depth to sustain change
  • Russia destabilizes successful cases (Ukraine 2014)
```

sections.text: ## Bridges: Revolution Theory as Systems Failure Analysis

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: Revolution theory's core models translate directly into systems failure analysis.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: **Skocpol's causal triangle → coupled-system failure mode**: The three conditions (fiscal stress, elite defection, peasant autonomy) are not independent failures — they are a coupled cascade. State fiscal crisis erodes the patronage that keeps elites loyal; elite defection removes the state's coercive enforcement capacity; autonomous peasant communities then exploit the enforcement gap. This is precisely the pattern in Perrow's *Normal Accidents* (1984): tightly coupled systems with hidden interdependencies fail catastrophically rather than gracefully when multiple components stress simultaneously. The key feature is that each failure mode amplifies the others. In distributed systems terms: the circuit breakers don't isolate the failure; instead, cascade propagation exhausts system capacity before any single node reaches its individual fault threshold.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: **Tilly's "revolutionary situation vs. outcome" → fault detection vs. fault propagation**: A revolutionary situation (dual sovereignty — two claimants to state power) is a detected fault: the system has entered an anomalous state, and all agents can observe the inconsistency. A revolutionary outcome is fault propagation that reaches a terminal state — the old regime's state apparatus dissolves and cannot be restored. Many detected faults are corrected before propagation (failed revolutions, stabilized crises); the question is whether the challenger coalition can sustain dual sovereignty long enough for state capacity to collapse irreversibly. In distributed systems: detecting split-brain is not the same as resolving it; the resolution depends on which partition can write to durable storage first.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: **Goldstone's demographic-structural model → resource exhaustion under load**: Population growth as a slow-moving variable that gradually saturates system capacity (fiscal, elite positional, subsistence) maps to long-term resource exhaustion under increasing load. The system appears stable until multiple resource pools hit limits simultaneously — not because any single limit was reached, but because the buffers that masked earlier stress were depleted. The "17th-century general crisis" (simultaneous state crises across Eurasia) is this pattern at continental scale: the same slow variable (population pressure) drove multiple systems to failure thresholds within the same generation.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: **Authoritarian reconsolidation post-revolution → thermidor as stable equilibrium restoration**: Post-revolutionary thermidor (Brinton's term for conservative reaction) is the system returning to a nearby stable equilibrium after being perturbed. The new equilibrium differs from the old (new ruling class, different institutional form) but shares key structural features (centralized coercive apparatus, elite-mass hierarchy). This is consistent with multiple-equilibria models: revolutions move between equilibria rather than creating entirely new ones.

metadata.title: Revolution Theory: Skocpol, Goldstone, Tilly, Arendt

sections.text: ## Why Some Revolutions Succeed: Synthesis

NECESSARY CONDITIONS (Skocpol-Goldstone)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. State fiscal/military crisis         │
  │ 2. Elite defection (old guard fractures)│
  │ 3. Mass mobilization capacity           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
               +
  SUFFICIENT CONDITIONS (Tilly + process)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 4. Security force defection or collapse │
  │    (army won't fire = regime falls)     │
  │ 5. Challenger coalition coherent enough │
  │    to build new state apparatus         │
  │ 6. International context permissive     │
  │    (no great-power intervention to      │
  │     restore old regime)                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
               =
  REVOLUTIONARY OUTCOME
  (Not just situation, but transfer +
   structural change)
